Perceiving his peril, the Pandavas endeavoured to rescue Arjuna's son; but Jayadratha held them back, and Karna aided him. At length Abhimanyu was wounded on the forehead, blood streamed into his eyes and blinded him, and he stumbled. Ere he could recover, the son of Duhsasana leapt forward and dashed out his brains with a mace. So died the gallant youth, pure as he was at birth. He died like to a forest lion surrounded by hunters; he sank like to the red sun at evening; he perished like to a tempest whose strength is spent; he was spent out even like a fire which has consumed a forest and is extinguished on the plain; Abhimanyu was lost as is the serene white moon when shrouded in black eclipse.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 58

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: So that day's battle ended, and Abhimanyu slumbered in the soft starlight, lifeless and cold.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 59

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: When it was told to Arjuna that his son was slain, the mighty warrior wept silently and lay upon the ground. At length he leapt up and cried: “May the curse of a father and the vengeance of a warrior smite the murderers of my boy!... May I never reach heaven if I do not slay Jayadratha on the morrow....” A spy hastened to the camp of the Kauravas and told of the vow which Arjuna had taken. Jayadratha trembled with fear.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 60

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Early next morning Arjuna spake to Krishna, saying: “Drive swiftly, for this will be a day of great slaughter.” He desired to find Jayadratha; with him went Bhima and Satyaki. Many warriors engaged them in battle, for the Kauravas hoped to contrive that the sun should go down ere Arjuna could fulfil his terrible vow.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 61

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Mounted on an elephant, Duhsasana opposed Arjuna; but the lordly tusker took flight when the rattling chariot drew nigh. Drona blocked the way; but Arjuna refused combat, saying: “Thou art as a father unto me.... Let me find the slayer of my son....” He passed on. Then Duryodhana came up and engaged him. Karna fought with Bhima, and Bhurisrava attacked Satyaki. Long waged the bitter conflicts, and at length Krishna perceived that his kinsman was about to be slain. He called to Arjuna, who cast a celestial weapon at Bhurisrava, which cut off both his arms; then Satyaki slew him. Many warriors confronted Arjuna thereafter, and many fell. But the day wore on and evening drew nigh, and he could not find Jayadratha. At length Arjuna bade Krishna to drive furiously onward, and to pause not until he found the slayer of his son. The chariot sped like to a whirlwind, until at length Arjuna beheld the evil-hearted Jayadratha; he was guarded by Karna and five great warriors, and at that time the sun had begun to set.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 62

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Karna leapt forward and engaged Arjuna; but Krishna, by reason of his divine power, caused a dark cloud to obscure the sun, whereupon all men believed that night had fallen. Karna at once withdrew; but Arjuna drove on, and as the sun shot forth its last ray of dazzling light, he dashed upon Jayadratha as a falcon swoops down upon its prey. Brief was the struggle, for ere daylight faded utterly, Arjuna overthrew the slayer of his son and cut off his head. Bhima uttered a roar of triumph when he saw the head of Jayadratha held aloft, and the Kauravas sorrowed greatly because that their wicked design had been thwarted.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 63

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Night fell, but the fighting was renewed. In the darkness and confusion men slew their kinsmen, fathers cut down their sons, and brothers fought against brothers. Yudhishthira sent men with torches to light up the blood-red plain, and the battle was waged for many hours. Swords were splintered and spears were lost, and warriors threw great boulders and chariot wheels against one another. All men were maddened with the thirst for blood, and the night was filled with horrors.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 64

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: At length Arjuna called for a truce, and it was agreed that the warriors should sleep on the battlefield. So all lay down, the charioteer in his chariot, the horseman on his steed, and the driver of the elephant on his elephant's back....
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 65

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Duryodhana reproached Drona because that he did not slay the Pandavas in their sleep.... “Let Karna,” he said, “lead the hosts to victory.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 66

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Said Drona: “Thou art reaping the red harvest of thy sins.... But know now that on the morrow either Arjuna will fall or I will be slain by him.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 67

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: When the bright moon rose in the heavens the conflict was renewed. Many fell on that awful night. Ghatotkacha, the Rakshasa son of Bhima, was foremost in the fray, and he slaughtered numerous Kaurava warriors. At length Karna went against him, and then the air was filled with blazing arrows. Each smote the other with powerful weapons, and for a time the issue hung in the balance. Ghatotkacha created illusions, but Karna kept his senses in that great fight, even after his steeds had been slain; he leapt to the ground, then flung a celestial dart, the gift of Indra, and Ghatotkacha, uttering terrible cries, fell down and breathed his last breath. The Kauravas shouted with gladness, and the Pandavas shed tears of sorrow.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 68

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Ere the night was ended, Drona slew his ancient enemy Drupada, Rajah of Southern Panchala, and he cut down also the Rajah of Virata.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 69

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Ere dawn broke, Dhrishta-dyumna, son of Drupada, went forth to search for Drona, the slayer of his beloved sire.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 70

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Said Bhima: “Thou art too young to strike down so great a warrior as Drona. I will fight with him until he is wearied, then thou canst approach and be avenged.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 71

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Bhima struggled with the sage, his preceptor, for many hours; then Dhrishta-dyumna engaged him, but neither could prevail over the slayer of Drupada.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 72

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: At length the Pandava warriors shouted falsely: “Aswatthaman, son of Drona, is slain.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 73

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: When Drona heard the dread tidings, he fainted in his chariot, and vengeful Dhrishta-dyumna rushed forward and cut off his head. Then the son of Drupada threw the head of Drona towards Duryodhana, saying: “Here is the head of thy mighty warrior; I will cut off the heads of each Kaurava prince in like manner.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 74

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: The fall of Drona was like the sinking of heaven's sun; it was like the drying up of the ocean; the Kauravas fled away in fear.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 75

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Terrible was the grief of Aswatthaman when he approached at eventide and found that his sire had been slain. Night fell while he sorrowed, and he vowed to slay Dhrishta-dyumna and all his kindred.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 76

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Karna was then chosen to be the leader of the Kaurava army, and Duryodhana hailed him with joy and said: “Thou alone canst stem the tide of our disasters. Arjuna hath been spared by Bhishma and by Drona because that they loved him. But the arm of Karna is strengthened by hatred of the proud Pandava archer.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 77

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: When morning broke over the plain of Kuru-kshetra, the first battle of Karna began, and it continued all day long. Countless warriors were slain; blood ran in streams, and the dead and mangled bodies of men and elephants and horses were strewn in confusion. The air was darkened with arrows and darts, and it rang with the shouts of the fighters and the moans of the wounded, the bellowing of trumpets, and the clamour of drums.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 78

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: At length evening came on and the carnage ended.... Duryodhana summoned a council of war and said: “This is the sixteenth day of the war, and many of our strongest heroes have fallen. Bhishma and Drona have fallen, and many of my brethren are now dead.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 79

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Said Karna: “To-morrow will be the great day of the war. I have vowed to slay Arjuna or fall by his hand.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 80

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Duryodhana was cheered by Karna's words, and all the Kauravas were once more hopeful of victory.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 81

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: In the morning Karna went forth in his chariot. He chose for his driver Salya, Rajah of Madra, whose skill was so great that even Krishna was not his superior.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 82

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Arjuna was again engaged in combat with Susarman when Karna attacked the Pandava army. So the son of Surya went against Yudhishthira and cast him on the ground, saying: “If thou wert Arjuna I would slay thee.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 83

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Bhima then attacked Karna, and they fought fiercely for a time, until Arjuna, having overcome Susarman, returned again to combat with Karna.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 84

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Duhsasana, who put Draupadi to shame, came up to help Karna, and Bhima sprang upon him. Now Bhima had long desired to meet this evil-hearted son of the blind maharajah, so that he might fulfil his vow. He swung his mace and struck so mighty a blow that the advancing chariot was shattered. Duhsasana fell heavily upon the ground and broke his back. Then Bhima seized him and, whirling his body aloft, cried out: “O Kauravas, come ye who dare and rescue the helper of Karna.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 85

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: No one ventured to approach, and Bhima cast down Duhsasana's body, cut off his head, and drank his blood as he had vowed to do. “Ho! ho!” he cried, “never have I tasted a sweeter draught....”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 86

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Many Kaurava warriors fled, and they cried out: “This is not a man, for he drinketh human blood.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 87

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: All men watched the deadly combat which was waged between the mighty heroes Arjuna and Karna. They began by shooting arrows one at another, while Krishna and Salya guided the chariots with prowess and care. The arrows of Arjuna fell upon Karna like to summer rain; Karna's arrows were like stinging snakes, and they drank blood. At length Arjuna's celestial bow Gandiva was struck and the bowstring severed....
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 88

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Arjuna said: “Pause, O Karna. According to the rules of battle, thou canst not attack a disabled foeman.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 89

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: But Karna heeded not. He showered countless arrows, until his proud rival was wounded grievously on the breast.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 90

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: When Arjuna had restrung his bow, he rose up like to a stricken and angry tiger held at bay, and cast a screen of arrows against his foe. But Karna feared him not, nor could Arjuna bear him down. The issue hung in the balance....
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 91

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Then suddenly a wheel of Karna's chariot sank in the soft ground, nor could Salya urge the horses to advance.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 92

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Karna cried out: “Pause now, O Arjuna, nor wage unequal war. It is not manly to attack a helpless enemy.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 93

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Arjuna paused; but Krishna spake quickly, saying: “O Karna, thou speakest truly; but was it manly to shoot arrows at Arjuna whilst he engaged himself restringing his bow? Was it manly to scoff at Draupadi when she was put to shame before elders and princes in the gambling hall? Was it manly of thee and six warriors to surround Abhimanyu so as to murder him without compassion?”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 94

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: When Arjuna heard his son's name, his heart burned with consuming wrath. Snatching from his quiver a crescent-bladed arrow, he drew his bow and shot it at Karna, whose head was immediately struck off.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 95

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: So fell in that dread combat a brother by a brother's hand.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 96

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: The Kauravas fled in terror when Karna was slain, and Kripa said unto Duryodhana: “Now that our greatest warriors are dead, it would be well to sue for peace.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 97

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Said Duryodhana: “After the wrongs I have done the Pandavas, how can I ask or expect mercy at their hands? Let the war go on till the end comes.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 98

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Salya was then chosen as the leader of the Kaurava army, which had greatly shrunken in numbers, and on the morning of the eighteenth day of the war the battle was waged with fury. But the Pandavas were irresistible, and when Duryodhana perceived that they were sweeping all before them, he fled away secretly, carrying his mace. He had power to hide under water as long as he desired, by reason of a mighty charm which had been conferred upon him by the demons; so he plunged into a lake and lay concealed below the waters.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 99

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Salya was slain by Yudhishthira, and he fell like to a thunder-splintered rock. Sahadeva overthrew false Shakuni, the gambler, who had played against Yudhishthira with loaded dice, and Bhima cut down all Duryodhana's brethren who had survived until that last fateful day. Of all the Kaurava heroes there then remained alive only Aswa-thaman, son of Drona, Kripa, and Kritavarman, and the hidden Duryodhana.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 100

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: At length Bhima discovered where Duryodhana was concealed. Yudhishthira went to the lake side and urged him to come forth and fight.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 101

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Said Duryodhana: “Take my kingdom now and have pleasure in it. Depart and leave me, for I must retire to the jungle and engage in meditation.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 102

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Yudhishthira said: “I cannot accept aught from thee except what is won in battle.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 103

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Said Duryodhana: “If you promise to fight one by one, I will come out of the water and slay you all.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 104

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Yudhishthira said: “Come forth, and the battle will be fought as thou dost desire. Now thou hast spoken as becomes a Kshatriya.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 105

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Still Duryodhana tarried, and Bhima shouted: “If thou dost not come out of the lake at once, I will plunge in and drag thee to the shore.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 106

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Then Duryodhana came forth, and the Pandavas laughed to see him, for he was covered with mire, and water streamed down from his raiment.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 107

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Said Duryodhana: “Soon will your merriment be turned to grief.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 108

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Now, all during the time of the Pandava exile, Duryodhana had practised with the mace, so that he became the equal of Bhima. But he had no one to support him there. The other survivors remained in hiding. Then Balarama appeared, and he caused the combat to be waged in the middle of the blood-red plain; he was Duryodhana's supporter.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 109

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: The warriors fought like two fierce bulls, and smote one another heavy blows, until their faces were reddened with blood. Once Duryodhana almost achieved victory, for he struck Bhima on the head so that all present thought that the Pandava hero had received his deathblow. Bhima staggered but recovered himself, and soon afterwards he struck Duryodhana a foul blow upon the knee, which smashed the bone so that he fell prostrate. Thus was the vow of Bhima fulfilled....
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 110

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: He danced round Duryodhana a time, then, kicking his enemy's head, cried out at length: “Draupadi is avenged.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 111

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Yudhishthira was wroth; he smote Bhima on the face and said: “O accursed villain, thou wilt cause all men to speak ill of us.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 112

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Then Arjuna led Bhima away, and Yudhishthira knelt beside Duryodhana and said: “Thou art still our ruler, and if thou wilt order me to slay Bhima, thy command will be obeyed. Thou art now very nigh unto death, and I sorrow for the Kaurava wives and children, who will curse us because that thou hast been laid low.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 113

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Said Balarama: “Bhima hath broken the laws of combat, for he smote Duryodhana below the waist.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 114

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Krishna said: “My brother, did not Duryodhana wrong the Pandavas with foul play at dice? And did not Bhima, when he beheld Draupadi put to shame, vow to break the knee of Duryodhana?”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 115

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Said Balarama: “So thou dost approve of this?... Can I forget that Bhima kicked the head of our wounded kinsman, the rajah?”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 116

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Krishna stayed the vengeful hand of Balarama, and prevailed upon him to take vows not to fight against the Pandavas.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 117

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: When night fell, the dying Duryodhana was visited on the battlefield by Aswatthaman, son of Drona, and Kripa, and Kritavarman. Unto Aswatthaman he gave permission to attack the Pandavas while yet they slumbered.... Then Drona's son went forth in the darkness to glut his hunger for vengeance because that his sire had been slain.... The pale stars looked down on the dead and the dying as Aswatthaman crossed the battleplain and went stealthily towards the tents of his foemen, with Kripa and Kritavarman.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 118

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: At the gate of the Pandava camp an awful figure rose up against the conspirators. Aswatthaman was not afraid, and he fought with his adversary until he perceived that he was the god Shiva, the Blue-throated Destroyer. Then Drona's son drew back, and on an altar he kindled a fire to worship the all-powerful deity. Then, having naught else to sacrifice, he cast his own body upon the flames. By this supremely pious act Shiva was propitiated; he accepted Drona's son and entered his body, saying: “Hitherto, for the sake of Krishna, have I protected the sons of Draupadi, but now their hour of doom hath come.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 119

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Then Aswatthaman rushed into the camp and slaughtered with the cruel arm of vengeance. Rudely he awakened Dhrishta-dyumna, who cried out: “Coward! wouldst thou attack a naked man?”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 120

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Aswatthaman answered not his father's slayer, but took his life with a single blow.... Through the camp he went, striking down each one he met, and shrieks and moans arose on every side.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 121

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Draupadi was awakened by the clamour, and her five young sons sprang up to protect her. Aswatthaman slew each one without pity.... Then he lit a great fire to discover those who had concealed themselves, and with reeking hands he completed his ghastly work of slaughter. Meanwhile Kripa and Kritavarman, with weapons in their hands, kept watch at the gate, and cut down all who endeavoured to escape.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 122

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Now the Pandava princes slept safely on that night of horror in the camp of the Kauravas, so that they escaped the sword of Drona's son.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 123

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: When his fell work was accomplished, the bloodthirsty Aswatthaman cut off the heads of Draupadi's five sons and carried them to Duryodhana, who rejoiced greatly, believing that they were the heads of Yudhishthira and his brethren. But when he perceived that the avenger of night had slain the children of Draupadi instead, he cried out: “Alas! what horror hast thou committed? Thou hast slain innocent children, who, had they lived, would have perpetuated our name and our fame. My heart burns with anger against the sires and not their harmless sons.”
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 124

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Duryodhana groaned heavily: his heart was oppressed with grief, and, bowing down his head, he died sorrowing.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 125

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Then Aswatthaman and Kripa and Kritavarman fled away, fearing the wrath of the Pandavas.
chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 19, Para 126

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XVIII: The Battle of Eighteen Days

text: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 1

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Draupadi's Sorrow—The Vengeful Maharajah—Bhima is Forgiven—Dead Burned on Battlefield—Atonement for Sin—The Horse Sacrifice—Arjuna's Wanderings—A Woman turned to Stone—The Amazons—Father and Son Conflict—The Wonderful Serpent Jewel—Return of the Horse—The Sacrifice Performed—Maharajah Retires to the Forest—Meeting of Mournful Relatives—The Vision of the Dead—Widows Drown Themselves—A Forest Tragedy—Dwaraka Horrors—End of Krishna and Balarama—City Destroyed by the Sea—Farewell of the Pandavas—The Journey to Heaven—Yudhishthira Tested by Deities—Vision of Hell—The Holy Life.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 2

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: When it was told to the Pandava brethren that their camp had been raided in darkness by the bloodthirsty Aswatthaman, Yudhishthira exclaimed: “Alas! sorrow upon sorrow crowds upon us, and now the greatest sorrow of all hath fallen. Draupadi mourns the death of her brother and her five sons, and I fear she will perish with grief.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 3

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Draupadi came before her husbands and, weeping bitterly, said: “For thirteen cruel years you have endured shame and exile so that your children might prosper. But now that they are all slain, can you desire to have power and kingdom?”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 4

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Said Krishna: “O daughter of a rajah, is thy grief so great as is Pritha's and Gandhari's, and as great as those who lament the loss or their husbands on the battlefield? Thou hast less cause than others to wail now.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 5

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Draupadi was soothed somewhat, but she turned to Bhima and said: “If thou wilt not bring to me the head of Aswatthaman, I will never again look upon thy face.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 6

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Said Yudhishthira: “Aswatthaman is a Brahman, and Vishnu, the greatest of the gods, will punish him if he hath done wrong. If we should slay him now, O Draupadi, thy sons and thy brother and thy sire would not be restored unto thee.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 7

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Draupadi said: “So be it. But Aswatthaman hath a great jewel which gleams in darkness. Let it be taken from him, for it is as dear unto him as his life.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 8

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Then Arjuna went in pursuit of Aswatthaman and found him, and returned with the jewel.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 9

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: To the battlefield came blind old Dhritarashtra, mourning the death of his hundred sons. And with the weeping maharajah were Queen Gandhari and the wives of the Kaurava princes, who sorrowed aloud. Wives wept for their husbands, their children wailed beside them, and mothers moaned for their sons. Bitter was the anguish of tender-hearted women, and the air was filled with wailing on that blood-red plain of Kuru-kshetra.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 10

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: When Queen Gandhari beheld the Pandavas she cried out: “The smell of Duryodhana is upon you all.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 11

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Now Dhritarashtra plotted in his weak mind to crush the head of Bhima, the slayer of Duryodhana. When he embraced Yudhishthira he said: “Where is Bhima?” and they placed before him an image of the strong Pandava. Dhritarashtra put forth his arms, and he crushed the image in his embrace and fell back fainting. Then he wailed: “Alas! Bhima was as a son unto me. Although I have slain him, the dead cannot return.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 12

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Well pleased was the maharajah when it was told to him that Bhima still lived; and he embraced his son's slayer tenderly and with forgiveness, saying: “I have no children now save the sons of Pandu, my brother.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 13

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Pritha rejoiced to meet her five sons, and she embraced them one by one. Then she went towards the sorrowing Draupadi, who fainted in her arms. Thereafter they wept together for the dead.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 14

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: The bodies of the slain rajahs and princes were collected together, and wrapped in perfumed linen and laid each upon a funeral pyre and burned, and the first pyre which was kindled was that of Duryodhana. The Pandavas mourned for their kinsmen. Then they bathed in the holy Ganges, and took up water and sprinkled it in the name of each dead hero. Yudhishthira poured out the oblation for Karna, his brother, and he gave great gifts to his widows and his children. Thereafter all the remaining bodies of the slain were burned on the battlefield.[285]
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 15

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Yudhishthira was proclaimed rajah in the city of Hastinapur, and he wore the great jewel in his crown. A great sacrifice was offered up, and Dhaumya, the family priest of the Pandavas, poured the Homa offering to the gods on the sacred fire. Yudhishthira and Draupadi were anointed with holy water.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 16

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: In the days that followed, Yudhishthira lamented over the carnage of the great war, nor could he be comforted. At length Vyasa, the sage, appeared before him and advised that he should perform the horse sacrifice to atone for his sins.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 17

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Then search was made for a moon-white horse with yellow tail and one black ear, and when it was found a plate of gold, inscribed with the name of Yudhishthira, was tied upon its forehead. Thereafter the horse was let loose, and was allowed to wander wheresoever it desired. A great army, which was led by Arjuna, followed the horse.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 18

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Now it was the custom in those days that when the sacred horse entered a raj[286], that raj was proclaimed to be subject to the king who performed the ceremony. And if any ruler detained the horse, he was compelled to fight with the army which followed the wandering animal. Should he be overcome in battle, the opposing rajah immediately joined forces with those of the conqueror, and followed the horse from kingdom to kingdom. For a whole year the animal was allowed to wander thus.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 19

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: The horse was let loose on the night of full moon in the month of Choitro.[287]
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 20

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Arjuna met with many adventures. He fought against a rajah and the son of a rajah, who had a thousand wives in the country of Malwa, and defeated them. But Agni, who had married a daughter of the rajah, came to rescue his kin. He fought against Arjuna with fire, but Arjuna shot celestial arrows which produced water. Then the god made peace, and the rajah who had detained the horse went away with Arjuna. Thereafter the horse came to a rock which was the girl-wife of a Rishi who had been thus transformed because of her wickedness. “So will you remain,” her husband had said, “until Yudhishthira performs the Aswa-medha ceremony.” The horse was unable to leave the rock. Then Arjuna touched the rock, which immediately became a woman, and the horse was set free.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 21

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: In time the horse entered the land of Amazons, and the queen detained it, and came forth with her women warriors to fight against Arjuna, who, however, made peace with them and went upon his way. Thereafter the holy steed reached a strange country where men and women and horses and cows and goats grew upon mighty trees like to fruit, and came to maturity and died each day. The rajah came against Arjuna, but was defeated. Then all the army fled to the islands of the sea, for they were Daityas, and Arjuna plundered their dwellings and obtained much treasure.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 22

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Once the horse entered a pond, and was cursed by the goddess Parvati, and it became a mare; it entered another pond and became a lion, owing to a Brahman's spell.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 23

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: In the kingdom of Manipura the horse was seized, and soldiers armed with fire weapons were ready to fight against the Pandavas and their allies. But when the rajah, whose name was Babhru-váhana, discovered that the horse bore the name of Yudhishthira, he said: “Arjuna is my sire;” and he went forth and made obeisance, and put his head under the foot of the Pandava hero. But Arjuna spurned him, saying: “If I were thy sire, thou wouldst have no fear of me.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 24

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Then the rajah challenged Arjuna to battle, and was victorious on that day.[288] He took all the great men prisoners, and he severed Arjuna's head from his body with a crescent-bladed arrow. The rajah's mother, Chitrangada, was stricken with sorrow, as was also Ulupi, the daughter of Vasuka, the king of serpents, who had borne a son to Arjuna. But Ulupi remembered that her sire possessed a magic jewel which had power to restore a dead man to life, and she sent the rajah of Manipura to obtain it from the underworld. But the Nagas refused to give up the jewel, whereupon Arjuna's mighty son fought against them with arrows which were transformed into peacocks; and the peacocks devoured the serpents. Then the Naga king delivered up the magic jewel, and the rajah returned with it. He touched the body of Arjuna with the jewel, and the hero came to life again, and all his wounds were healed. When he departed from Manipura city the rajah, his son, accompanied him.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 25

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: So from kingdom to kingdom the horse wandered while the army followed, until a year had expired. Then it returned to Hastinapur.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 26

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Yudhishthira had meantime lived a life of purity and self-restraint. Each night he lay upon the ground, and always slept within the city. Beside him lay Draupadi, and a naked sword was ever betwixt them.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 27

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Great were the rejoicings of the people when the horse came back: they made glad holiday, and went forth to welcome the army with gifts of fine raiment and jewels and flowers. Money was scattered in the streets, and the poor were made happy, being thus relieved generously in their need.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 28

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Yudhishthira embraced Arjuna and kissed him and wept tears of gladness, and welcomed Arjuna's son, Babhru-váhana, Rajah of Manipura, and also the other rajahs who had followed the sacred horse.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 29

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Twelve days after the return of Arjuna, and on the day when Magha's full moon marked the close of the winter season, the people assembled in great multitudes from far and near to share Yudhishthira's generous hospitality and witness the Aswa-medha ceremony, which was held upon a green and level portion of consecrated ground. Stately pavilions, glittering with jewels and gold, had been erected for the royal guests, and there were humbler places for the Brahmans. In thrones of gold sat Maharajah Dhritarashtra and Rajah Yudhishthira, and the other rajahs had thrones of sandalwood and gold. The royal ladies were ranged together in their appointed places. Wise Vyasa was there, and he directed the ceremony. And Krishna, the holy one, was there also.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 30

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: When all the guests were assembled, Yudhishthira and Draupadi bathed together in the sacred waters of the Ganges. Then a portion of ground was measured out, and Yudhishthira ploughed it with a golden plough. Draupadi followed him, and sowed the seeds of every kind which is sown in the kingdom, while all the women and the Brahmans chanted holy mantras. Then a golden altar was erected with four broad layers of golden bricks, and stakes of sacred wood from the forest and from Himalaya, and it was canopied and winged with gold-brocaded silk.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 31

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Then eight pits were dug for Homa[289] of milk and butter to be made ready for the sacrificial fire, and in skins were wrapped up portions of every kind of vegetable and curative herb which grew in the kingdom, and these were placed in the Homa pits.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 32

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: On the ground there were numerous sacrificial stakes, to which were tied countless animals—bulls and buffaloes and steeds, wild beasts from forest and mountain and cave, birds of every kind, fishes from river and lake, and even insects.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 33

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: The priests offered up animals in sacrifice to each celestial power, and the feasting was beheld by sacred beings. The Gandharvas sang, and the Apsaras, whom the Gandharvas wooed, danced like sunbeams on the grass. Messengers of the gods were also gathered there, and Vyasa and his disciples chanted mantras to celestial music. The people lifted up their voices at the sound of rain drum and the blast of the rain trumpet. Then bright was the lustre of Yudhishthira's fame.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 34

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: When all the kings and royal ladies and sages took their places to be blessed by the horse sacrifice, Yudhishthira sat on his throne, and in his hand he held the horn of a stag.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 35

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Vyasa sent four-and-sixty rajahs with their wives to draw water from the holy Ganges. Many musicians went with them beating drums and blowing trumpets and playing sweet instruments, and girls danced in front, going and returning. And all the rajahs and their wives were given splendid raiment by Yudhishthira, and necklaces of jewels also, and he put betelnut in their mouths one by one. To the Brahmans were gifted much gold and many jewels, and elephants, horses, and kine, and they were well pleased.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 36

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Yudhishthira then sat naked in his throne, and each one who had drawn holy water poured a quantity over his head; and they poured what remained over the head of the sacred white horse.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 37

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Nákula held the horse's head, and said: “The horse speaketh.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 38

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Those who were about him asked in loud voices: “What doth the horse reveal?”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 39

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Said Nákula: “Thus speaketh the horse—‘In other such ceremonies the horse which is sacrificed departs unto Swarga[290], but I shall rise far above Swarga, because that Krishna is here’.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 40

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Then Dhaumya, having washed the horse, gave a scimitar to Bhima with which to strike off the head at a single blow. But ere this was done, Dhaumya pressed an ear of the holy animal, and milk flowed forth. Then he said to Bhima: “Pure indeed is the horse; verily the gods will accept the sacrifice. Strike now, O strong one.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 41

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Bhima raised the scimitar and severed the head, which immediately ascended unto heaven and vanished from before the eyes of all. Great was the wonder and the joy of the assembled multitude.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 42

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Krishna and other rajahs and sages then cut open the horse's body, from which a bright light issued forth. They found that the animal was pure, and Krishna said unto Yudhishthira: “This, thy sacrifice, is acceptable unto Vishnu.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 43

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Draupadi was made Queen of the Sacrifice, and mantras were chanted, and she was adored and given rich offerings, because of her virtue and her wisdom.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 44

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: The body of the slain steed was divided, and the flesh gave forth the odour of camphor. Priests lifted portions in their ladles and placed these on the sacrificial fire, and they made Soma. And Rajah Yudhishthira and all his brethren stood in the sin-cleansing smoke and breathed its fragrance.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 45

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Dhaumya cried out, as he laid a piece of flesh on the altar fire: “O Indra, accept thou this flesh which hath turned to camphor.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 46

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: When he had uttered these words, Indra, accompanied by many gods, appeared before the people, who made obeisance with fear and secret joy. Indra took from Vyasa portions of the flesh and gave these to each of the gods. Then he vanished from sight with all his companions.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 47

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Vyasa blessed Yudhishthira, and Krishna embraced him.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 48

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Said Krishna: “Thy fame will endure for ever.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 49

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Yudhishthira made answer: “Unto thee do I owe all these blessings.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 50

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Thereafter Krishna and the rajahs poured holy water over the heads of Yudhishthira and Draupadi.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 51

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: All the fragments of the herbs which had been provided for Homa were then ground into powder. And Yudhishthira gave balls of the powder to each one present, so that they might eat of the sacred herbs and share in the blessings of the Aswa-medha. He ate his own portion last of all. The fragments of the offerings which remained were burnt on the altar.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 52

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Then Pritha and all the maidens who were with her made merry, while the musicians played gladsome airs.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 53

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Yudhishthira distributed more gifts. Unto Vyasa he assigned an estate, and bestowed upon the Brahmans who officiated many animals and pearls and slaves. To the rajahs he gave war elephants and steeds and money, and to the rajahs' wives bridal-night gifts of raiment and jewels and gold.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 54

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Bhima feasted all the Brahmans, and Yudhishthira wept as he bade farewell to Krishna, his friend in peace and in war, who departed in his chariot unto sea-washed Dwaraka.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 55

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: There was prosperity in the kingdom under Yudhishthira's wise and just government; but blind old Dhritarashtra never ceased to mourn the death of Duryodhana, his first-born, and at length he retired to live in a humble dwelling in the jungle. With him went Queen Gandhari, and Pritha, the mother of the Pandavas, and Vidura, and others who were of great age.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 56

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Years went past, and a day came when Yudhishthira and his brethren and their wife Draupadi journeyed to the dwelling-place of their elders. They found them all there save Vidura, who had departed to a sacred place on the banks of the Ganges to undergo penance and wait for the coming of Yama, god of the dead. Then all the kinsfolk, young and old, went forth to find Vidura; but when they came to him he was wasted with hunger and great age, nor could he speak unto them. They waited beside him until he died, and then they mourned together. This new sorrow awakened old-time grief, and they spoke of all those who had fallen in the great war. Fathers and mothers lamented for their sons, and wives for their husbands....
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 57

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: While they wept and moaned together, the great sage Vyasa came nigh and spoke, saying: “Verily, I will soothe all your sorrows.... Let each one bathe at sunset in the holy waters of the Ganges, and when night falls your lost ones will return to you once again.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 58

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Then they all sat waiting on the river bank until evening came on. Slowly passed the day; it seemed to be as long as a year.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 59

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: At length the sun went down, and they chanted mantras and went into the Ganges. Vyasa bathed beside the old Maharajah Dhritarashtra and Yudhishthira.... Then all came out and stood on the bank.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 60

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Suddenly the waters began to heave and foam, and Vyasa muttered holy words and called out the names of the dead one by one.... Soon all the heroes who had been slain arose one by one. In chariots they came, and on horseback and riding upon lordly elephants. They all uttered triumphant cries; drums were sounded and trumpets were blown; and it seemed as if the armies of the Pandavas and Kauravas were once again assembled for battle, for they swept over the river like a mighty tempest.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 61

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Many of the onlookers trembled with fear, until they beheld Bhishma and Drona, clad in armour, standing aloft in their chariots in splendour and in pride; then came Arjuna's son, the noble Abhimanyu, and Bhima's Asura son. Soon Gandhari beheld Duryodhana and all his brethren, while Pritha looked with glad eyes upon Karna, and Draupadi welcomed her brother Dhrishta-dyumna and her five children who had all been slain by vengeful Aswatthaman. All the warriors who had fallen in battle returned again on that night of wonder.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 62

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: With the host came minstrels who sang of the deeds of the heroes, and beautiful girls who danced before them. All strife had ended between kinsmen and old-time rivals; in death there was peace and sweet companionship.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 63

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: The ghostly warriors crossed the Ganges and were welcomed by those who waited on the bank around Vyasa. It was a night of supreme and heart-stirring gladness. Fathers and mothers found their sons, widows clung to their husbands, sisters embraced their brothers, and all wept tears of joy. The elders who were living conversed with those who were dead; the burdens of grief and despair fell from all hearts after lone years of mourning; the past was suddenly forgotten in the rapture of beholding those who had died.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 64

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Swiftly passed the night as if it had endured but for an hour. Then when dawn began to break, the dead men returned to their chariots and their horses and their elephants and bade farewells....
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 65

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Vyasa spoke to the widows and said that those of them who desired to be with their husbands could depart with them. Then the Kaurava princesses and other high-born ladies, who never ceased to mourn for their own, kissed the feet of the Maharajah Dhritarashtra and Queen Gandhari and plunged into the Ganges with the departing hosts.... Vyasa chanted mantras, and all the drowned widows were transported to heaven with their husbands....
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 66

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: The Pandavas returned to Hastinapur, and when two years had gone past a new sorrow fell upon them. One day Narada, the sage, stood before Yudhishthira and told that a great fire had swept through the jungle, and that Dhritarashtra, and Gandhari, and Pritha, and all who were with them, had perished.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 67

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Soon afterwards the Pandavas came to know, by reason of dread omens which appeared, that a great calamity was drawing nigh, but no man could tell what it was or when it would take place.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 68

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Ere long it became known that the city of Dwaraka was doomed to be destroyed. A horror in human shape was beheld in the night; it was coloured yellow and black, its head was bald and its limbs misshapen, and men said it was Yama, god of the dead.... Visions of headless men contending in battle were beheld at sunset.... The moon was eclipsed, a dread tempest ravaged the land, and a plague of rats afflicted the city.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 69

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Krishna forbade all the people, on pain of death, to drink wine, and commanded them to perform devotions on the seashore....
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 70

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Then the night was haunted by a black woman with yellow teeth who grinned horribly at house doors. All the inhabitants of the city were stricken with terror.... Evil spirits came also and robbed the jewels of the women and the weapons of the men.... At length the chakra[291] of Krishna went up to heaven, and his chariot and horses followed it.... The end of the Yádavas was not afar off, and the day came when Apsaras called out of heaven: “Depart from hence,” and all the people heard them.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 71

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: When the people gathered on the seashore they held a feast, and being allowed to drink wine for one day, they drank heavily and began to quarrel. At length Satyaki slew Kritavarman, who had gone to the Pandava camp with Drona's son on the night of slaughter. Then Kritavarman's friends killed Satyaki and one of Krishna's sons. Krishna slew the rebels, but he could not quell the tumult and the fighting which ensued; fathers slew their sons, and sons their fathers, and kinsmen contended fiercely against kinsmen.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 72

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Then Krishna and Balarama left the city, and both died in the jungle. From Balarama's mouth issued a mighty snake, for he was the incarnation of the world serpent.... Krishna was mistaken for a gazelle by a hunter, who shot an arrow which pierced his foot at the only spot where he could be mortally wounded. He then departed to his heaven, which is called Goloka.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 73

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Ere Krishna had left Dwaraka he caused messengers to hasten for Arjuna, who came speedily, to find the women wailing for the dead. Then Vasudeva, father of Krishna, died, and Arjuna laid the body of the old man upon the pyre, and he was burned with four of his widows, who no longer desired to live. The bodies of Krishna and Balarama were cremated also.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 74

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Arjuna then set forth towards Indra-prastha with a remnant of the people; and when they had left Dwaraka, the sea rose up and swallowed the whole city, with those who had refused to depart from it.... Such was the end of the power of the Yadavas.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 75

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Deep gloom fell upon the Pandavas after this, and Vyasa, the sage, appeared before them, and revealed that their time had come to depart from the world.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 76

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Then Yudhishthira divided the kingdom. He made Parikshit, son of Abhimanyu, Rajah of Hastinapur; and Yuyutsu, the half-brother of Duryodhana, who had joined the Pandava army on the first day of the great war, was made Rajah of Hastinapur. He counselled them to live at peace one with another.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 77

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: The Pandavas afterwards cast off their royal garments and their jewels and put on the garb of hermits, and the bright-eyed and faithful Draupadi did likewise. Yudhishthira departed first of all, and his brethren walked behind him one by one, and Draupadi went last of all, followed by a hound. They all walked towards the rising sun, and by the long circuitous path which leads to Mount Meru, through forests and over streams and across the burning plains, never again to return.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 78

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: One by one they fell by the way, all save Yudhishthira. Draupadi was the first to sink down, and Bhima cried: “Why hath she fallen who hath never done wrong?”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 79

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Said Yudhishthira: “Her heart was bound up in Arjuna, and she hath her reward.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 80

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Sahadeva was next to fall, and then Nakula. At length Yudhishthira heard the voice of Bhima crying in distress: “Lo! now the noble Arjuna hath fallen. What sin hath he committed?”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 81

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Said Yudhishthira: “He boasted confidently that he could destroy all his enemies in one day, and because he failed in his vow he hath fallen by the way.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 82

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: The two surviving brothers walked on in silence; but the time came when mighty Bhima sank down. He cried: “O Yudhishthira say, if thou canst tell, why I have fallen now.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 83

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Said Yudhishthira: “O wolf-bellied one, because of thy cursing and gluttony and thy pride thou hast fallen by the way.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 84

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Yudhishthira walked on, calm and unmoved, followed by his faithful hound. When he drew nigh to sacred Mount Meru, the world-spine, Indra, king of the gods, came forth to welcome him, saying: “Ascend, O resolute prince.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 85

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Said Yudhishthira: “Let my brethren who have fallen by the way come with me also. I cannot enter heaven without them, O king of the gods. Let the fair and gentle princess come too; Draupadi hath been a faithful wife, and is worthy of bliss. Hear my prayer, O Indra, and have mercy.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 86

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Said Indra: “Thy brethren and Draupadi have gone before thee.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 87

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Then Yudhishthira pleaded that his faithful hound should enter heaven also; but Indra said: “Heaven is no place for those who are followed by hounds. Knowest thou not that demons rob religious ordinances of their virtues when dogs are nigh?”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 88

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Said Yudhishthira: “No evil can come from the noble. I cannot have joy if I desert this faithful friend.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 89

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Indra said: “Thou didst leave behind thy brethren and Draupadi. Why, therefore, canst thou not abandon thine hound?”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 90

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Said Yudhishthira: “I have no power to bring back to life those who have fallen by the way: there can be no abandonment of the dead.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 91

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: As he spake, the hound was transformed, and behold Dharma, god of justice, stood by the rajah's side.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 92

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Dharma said: “O Yudhishthira, thou art indeed mine own son. Thou wouldst not abandon me, thy hound, because that I was faithful unto thee. Thine equal cannot be found in heaven.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 93

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Then Yudhishthira was transported to the city of eternal bliss, and there he beheld Duryodhana seated upon a throne. All the Kauravas were in heaven also, but the rajah could not find his brethren or fair Draupadi.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 94

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Said Indra: “Here thou shalt dwell, O Yudhishthira, in eternal bliss. Forget all earthly ties and attain to perfection; thy brethren have fallen short, therefore they sank by the way.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 95

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Yudhishthira said: “I cannot remain here with the Kauravas who have done me great wrong. Where my brethren are, there would I be also with our wife Draupadi.”
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 96

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Then a celestial being conducted Yudhishthira to the abode of his brethren and the Princess of Panchala. He entered the forest of the nether regions, where the leaves were like to sharp weapons and the path was covered with knives. Darkness hung heavily, and the way was miry with blood and strewn with foul and mutilated corpses. Shapes of horror flitted round about like to shadows; fierce birds of prey feasted upon human flesh. The damned were burning in everlasting fires, and the air reeked with foul odours. A boiling river went past, and Yudhishthira saw the place of torture with thorns, and the desert of fiery sand: he gazed mutely upon each horror that was unfolded before his eyes.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 97

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Fain would Yudhishthira have turned back, but he heard in the darkness the voices of his brethren and Draupadi bidding him to stay a little while to comfort them while they suffered torment.
chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven
source_reference: Indian Myth and Legend (Mackenzie 1913), Ch 20, Para 98

metadata.chapter_title: Chapter XIX: Atonement and the Ascent to Heaven

text: Then Yudhishthira said to the celestial being: “Depart now from me, for I must remain here to assuage the sufferings of my brethren and Draupadi.”
